x_intro_ext_sentence: In the aggregate, then, there is no trade-off between the externalities: by cutting use, the screen keeps more children out of a shelter than it sends to one by putting their parents out. What the \emph{budget, earnings and childhood homelessness externalities} have to outweigh is only the direct loss to the parent from the removal of an option. As I explain below, even the parent gains once general-equilibrium effects are taken into account.
x_intro_gain: A newborn gains $2.57$ percent of lifetime consumption. About $64$ percent of that gain comes in childhood, from a parent who spends more on the child's consumption and housing and less on drugs, and is less likely to remain unemployed longer because of a SUD, further improving childhood consumption. About $18$ percent comes from the higher earnings of a child whose parent was free of the disorder. The remaining $17$ percent comes from a better economy to live in as an adult: whatever its productivity, an eligible household that stays clean is $16$ percent more likely to get a voucher, paid for by the users the screen excludes and by the higher taxes paid by working-age households that no longer carry the earnings penalty or remain unemployed longer because of a SUD. Lastly, even some drug users benefit from the lower equilibrium drug price, with $24$ percent of the households that have a SUD better off on net in the long run, despite losing access to vouchers.

x_lr_adult:
The other $36$ percent comes in adult life, from two sources. The first, $18$ percent of the whole gain, is the better productivity node a child draws, mostly because its own parent does not carry the disorder. Escaping the penalty is worth a lot to each child it spares, about $55$ times what the average child gains at the same productivity. But it spares only about $2$ percent of children, since the share of newborns who enter adult life with the penalty falls from $8.99$ to $7.37$ percent.

The second, the remaining $17$ percent, does not come from the child's productivity at all. It is a result of the better economy it lives its adult life in. A clean and eligible household is $16$ percent more likely to draw a voucher.

Third, the vouchers Treatment First revokes from households with a SUD go, through a higher $\pi_V$, to other low-income households.
